newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland sets out rules for significant state firms.
newsitem.headline: Poland sets out rules for significant state firms.

text.p: The Polish cabinet has designated more than 200 state owned or controlled firms which have special economic significance and adopted new rules on their management or privatisation, a senior official said on Tuesday.
The rules adopted on December 23, are part of a major, long-running reform of ministries and administration, partly aimed at reducing central government's role in the economy.

Marek Pol, cabinet plenipotentiary in charge of the reform, told a news conference: "One of the most significant of the (December 23) cabinet decisions sets out a list of state-owned firms and of joint stock companies fully owned by the treasury which have special significance for the state economy.".
He said 90 state enterprises and 124 treasury-owned joint-stock companies would get special status, but did not name them and said details would be published in a government bulletin.
"Any such enterprise can be privatised only through a decision by the cabinet," Pol said.
He said only the supervisory board could appoint the management of such a firm, and not the heads of ministries overseeing the companies.

The appointment of the supervisory board and the drawing up of these companies' internal regulations would be subject to decisions by two ministers -- the treasury minister and one other -- in most cases the economy minister.
The economy ministry, to be headed by former privatisation minister Wieslaw Kaczmarek, is one of two major portfolios set to arise on Wednesday January 1.
The privatisation ministry was axed on October 1 and many of its responsibilities were taken over by the powerful new treasury ministry under Miroslaw Pietrewicz.

Among other changes taking effect on Wednesday, the sprawling, diversified Office of the Council of Ministers (cabinet) portfolio will be scrapped and make way for a new Ministry of the Interior and Administration.

Under the reform, on October 1 about 1,300 of Poland's remaining state-owned firms were placed under provincial governors rather than central government -- a move designed to hasten their privatisation. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
